sections.body:
What is constructive feedback?

Constructive feedback helps people understand the effect their actions are having and gives them a foundation to improve. It is specific, timely and grounded in observable behaviour rather than personal judgement. For graduates and apprentices, your observations are often the most direct development signal they receive — which makes your approach as important as the content of what you say.

The SBI model

Use Situation–Behaviour–Impact (SBI) to keep your feedback specific and fair:

  • Situation: When and where did this happen? A specific moment prevents the conversation feeling like a verdict on the person.
  • Behaviour: What exactly did you observe — what was said, written or done? Describe the action, not your interpretation of why.
  • Impact: What effect did it have on the team, the client, the work or the candidate's development?

After stating the impact, pause. Invite a response before moving to next steps.

Listening before solving

Once you have opened the conversation, your role shifts to listener. Resist the urge to fill silences or move straight to guidance. Ask an open question — 'What is your take on what I have described?' — before offering solutions. If the conversation surfaces signs of difficulty, ask whether anything is making the work harder at the moment, then know what your firm can offer if the answer suggests a need beyond your role to address.

How would you open this conversation?

A graduate has submitted a report. The recommendations are listed without any cost or programme context. The client reads that section first. Before reading on, consider: how would you open the feedback conversation?

A vague opening — 'The recommendations could be clearer, have another look' — leaves the graduate with nothing specific to act on. A specific one anchors the feedback in something observable: 'In the executive summary you submitted on Tuesday, the recommendations didn't include cost or programme context. The client reads that first, so without it they may not understand what action is needed or how urgent it is. What was your thinking when you wrote that section?' The difference is that the second version opens a conversation; the first closes one.

What would you do if they went quiet?

You have stated the impact. The person goes quiet for ten seconds. Before reading on, consider: would you wait, or would you speak?

Filling the silence too quickly risks taking over a conversation that belongs to both of you. Waiting — even through a long pause — signals that you are genuinely listening. If they still find it difficult to respond, a simple open question — 'What is your take on what I have described?' — usually helps.

Four common reactions: someone who is defensive needs you to stay with the specific behaviour, calmly, rather than engaging with their response to it. Someone who is upset needs a pause and an acknowledgement — 'I can see this is difficult' — before you continue. Someone who agrees too quickly needs a follow-up: 'What would you change specifically?' Someone who is withdrawn needs time and an open question before anything else.

sections.practicePrompt: Jordan Marsh is an eight-month degree apprentice on the Building Surveying pathway. You have arranged this meeting to give feedback on the quality of Jordan's written survey reports. Use the SBI model to open the conversation and invite Jordan to share their perspective. Jordan's personal circumstances are not known to you — approach this as you would any early-career colleague.

practiceCharacter.scenarioContext:
Jordan Marsh is 21 years old and eight months into a four-year Building Surveying BSc degree apprenticeship at a mid-sized surveying and construction consultancy. Jordan came through a vocational route at school and is the first person in their immediate family to work in a professional office environment. Jordan is genuinely enthusiastic about the work, particularly anything involving site visits and inspection. However, the professional written output expected at firm level is markedly different from what Jordan experienced at college and in the academic element of the apprenticeship, and Jordan has not fully grasped this gap.

The specific issue: over the past two months, Jordan has submitted four survey reports in which action points were buried in body text rather than clearly signposted, prioritisation was absent, and recurring grammatical errors made some sections difficult to read. Jordan's supervisor gave informal written guidance on the second report and verbal guidance after the third. The fourth report, submitted last week, showed only marginal improvement. This is the first time Jordan has been asked to meet specifically about the reports.

What Jordan knows entering this meeting: the manager asked to meet to catch up on how things are going. Jordan did not receive any indication that this was a feedback conversation and is not expecting specific criticism. Jordan has been dimly aware that the reports might not be perfect but has not understood the seriousness of the gap.

Jordan's internal state: low-level, background anxiety about whether they are good enough for the role — imposter syndrome, though Jordan would not use that term. Jordan genuinely does not understand what professional report writing looks like at the standard the firm expects. The feedback on the second report felt vague and Jordan is not sure what specifically to change. Jordan has been meaning to ask a colleague for a report example to work from but has not done so because they fear looking incompetent.

How Jordan is likely to respond at different points in the conversation:
- If the manager opens with specific, calm SBI feedback, Jordan will listen carefully but respond cautiously at first — something like 'I didn't realise it was that noticeable' or 'I thought the last one was better.'
- If the manager asks for Jordan's perspective before jumping to solutions, Jordan is likely to become more candid — admitting to finding the professional format confusing, or harder than expected from university. Jordan might say something like 'I'm not always sure what level of detail you want' or 'I think I write it more like an essay and I know that's probably not right.'
- If the manager asks an open question about whether anything is making the work harder, Jordan may say that the transition from education to professional writing has been harder than expected, and that they haven't felt comfortable asking for help.
- If the manager is blunt, prescriptive or makes Jordan feel judged rather than supported, Jordan will shut down: shorter answers, surface agreement without real engagement — 'Okay, I'll try to do better.'
- If the manager asks what support would help, Jordan will respond positively to concrete suggestions — a report example, a template, someone to review a draft before submission.

What Jordan needs from this conversation: clear, specific guidance on what professional report writing looks like at firm standard — ideally a concrete mechanism such as example reports, a template, or a more experienced colleague to review a draft before submission. Jordan needs to understand that the standard is achievable, not just that the current output is insufficient. Jordan would also benefit from an agreed next step — a check-in date, a draft review, or access to examples — that feels supportive rather than performative.

Boundaries: Jordan will not disclose personal health information, significant family circumstances, or anything of a genuinely private nature in a conversation with a line manager they have known for eight months. If the manager asks directly about personal circumstances in an intrusive way, Jordan will deflect politely: 'I'd rather not get into personal stuff — I'm fine, it's just been a complicated few weeks.' Jordan is willing to admit professional difficulty — not understanding the format, not knowing how to ask for help — if the conversation has been conducted with genuine respect.

Tone: respond as Jordan would — two to three sentences at a time. Sound like a thoughtful young professional trying to hold themselves together. Not dramatic, not perfectly open, not entirely closed off. Never break character, never offer coaching to the manager, never acknowledge being an AI.

sections.body:
Preparing for a real feedback conversation

Use the questions below to plan an upcoming feedback conversation with someone in your team. Work through them in your own notes — this is a planning exercise for your own development, not a formal record.

Important: Do not record personal information about the person you are thinking of. Focus only on the observable situation and what you plan to say. Notes you make here are for your own preparation and should not be retained as a performance or HR record.

Identify the situation

  • What specific event or pattern of behaviour do you want to address?
  • When and where did it occur? Be as specific as the situation allows.

Frame the behaviour

  • What exactly did you observe? Can you describe it without interpreting motivation or personality?
  • If you found yourself using an evaluative word — careless, disengaged, unreliable — what was the actual thing you saw or heard that prompted that word?

Consider the impact

  • What effect has this had — on the work, the team, the client relationship, or the candidate's professional development?
  • Can you state the impact factually, without overstating it?

Anticipate the response

  • How do you expect the person to react? What would you do if they became defensive? What if they became upset?
  • Is there anything that might be contributing to the issue that you are not currently aware of? What open question could you ask to find out?

Plan the follow-up

  • What would a reasonable next step look like — a revised piece of work, a check-in conversation, an introduction to a buddy or mentor?
  • When will you follow up, and how will you both know that progress has been made?

Practical logistics

  • Where will you have this conversation? Is it private?
  • How much time will you allow? Most informal feedback conversations benefit from an unrushed pace — aim for at least twenty minutes.
  • Is there anything you need to know or prepare first — for example, whether a formal process is already in place, or whether HR guidance would be appropriate?

sections.reflectionPrompt: Think back over the practice conversation you just completed. What felt natural, and where did you notice yourself struggling? Consider: how specific was your use of SBI? Did you give Jordan space to respond, or did you move too quickly to solutions? Now think about the real conversation you are preparing for. What one thing would you do differently, and why?
